description: We’re five students from Tustin, California who want to make hard ideas easier to understand. We chose the Space Mission Design Game because of one question: what if the person running a space mission had never done it before? That became our game, How Did We Get Here? Our Lead Programmer, Head Writer, Art Designer, Video Editor, and Science & Data Lead all learned the science as we built it. Players can start unqualified, make mistakes, and pick up real mission vocabulary along the way.
summary:
How Did We Get Here? is a story-driven game that puts you in the seat of a mission designer who has never done this before. The Chief Mission Designer has quit, and a General needs a mission launched on schedule. You choose a destination (the Moon, Mars or Venus), design a spacecraft, and balance six limits real NASA teams face: budget, mass, power, communications, data and mission lifetime. Then you build, launch and fly it. A mission report explains what happened, like a scientist’s notebook.
Our innovation is that what your character knows is the difficulty, and your character learns from failure. Most mission games assume you’re already an expert, but the hardest part of space is the vocabulary.
Three voices, one decision. An inner voice gives hints that depend on who you picked. The Assistant Scientist names the real term and number, The Janitor uses everyday comparisons, and The Student only asks questions.
The voice learns. When a mission fails, your character earns the word for the main cause and saves it in a Notebook. Later hints use that word.
In most mission games, you win by knowing the answers. In ours, you win by learning them. Your character starts out knowing very little, and each failed mission teaches a new term, so by the end anyone can think like a mission designer.

What inspired us. Most people only see the finished rocket, not the thousands of decisions behind it. We wanted anyone, even someone with no space background, to feel what it is like to be handed an impossible job and still make it work. We also noticed that the hardest part of space for most people isn’t the thinking, it’s the vocabulary: payload, orbit, data rate, trade-off. So we built a game where you start out unqualified, the way many of us feel when we first look at a real NASA mission, and learn the words by designing, failing and trying again.

How it works. The Chief Mission Designer has quit, and a random person is put in charge: The Assistant Scientist (easy), The Janitor (medium) or The Student (hard). Players pick a mission and a science goal: listening for moonquakes, finding water ice on Mars, or studying storms on Venus. In the Design Lab they choose the science instruments, a rocket and an orbit, and watch six resources push against each other: budget, mass, power, communications, data and mission lifetime. Every choice costs something. A heavier spacecraft needs a bigger rocket, which costs more money. A bigger battery can survive a long night but adds mass. After a Review step, players build the spacecraft in three hands-on minigames, launch it, fly it, and do the science. At the end, a mission report scores the run out of 1,000 and explains what went wrong, why, and how to fix it. A failed mission is a lesson, not a game over.

What is innovative. Other mission design games assume the player is already an expert. In ours, what the character knows is the difficulty, and the character learns from failure. An inner voice guides each decision, and it only knows what that character knows. The Assistant Scientist names the real term and gives a real number. The Janitor compares the choice to everyday life with no technical words. The Student asks a question about the trade-off and never gives the answer. When a mission fails, the game finds the main cause (for example, a spacecraft too heavy for its rocket) and the character earns the word for it, such as “payload capacity.” The word goes into a saved Notebook with a short meaning and a line about the player’s own run, and the character uses it in later hints. Each character keeps its own Notebook, so failing becomes a way of learning.

Use of NASA data. The game’s numbers come from real missions, and every value in our data files has its source recorded, so a player or teacher can trace it back to NASA. For example:

  • The Mars orbit fuel is based on Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter’s real fuel load, and its signal and mission length limits come from the mission’s JPL press kit.
  • The Moon’s seismometer power is based on the Apollo 15 Passive Seismic Experiment.
  • The Venus cloud camera power is based on the Pioneer Venus Cloud Photopolarimeter.
  • Rocket costs come from NASA launch contracts: Falcon 9 from the PACE mission, Atlas V 401 from Lucy, and Atlas V 541 from Mars 2020.

The hint numbers aren’t typed into the text. The game pulls them from its data files when a hint appears, so each hint matches the mission on screen.

Why it matters. Mission design is teamwork and trade-offs, and a game can teach both. We hope players leave understanding why real missions cost what they do, why “just add more” never works in space, and that curiosity plus careful planning can take you anywhere, even if you started out as the janitor.

Tools used: Claude Code (Anthropic), ChatGPT image generation, and the Godot game engine.

  • Game assembly (Godot). The game was put together and run in Godot. Godot is a game engine, not an SI tool. It was used to combine the scripts, art, audio, and data into the finished game. The Lead Programmer ran and tested the game in Godot at every step.
  • Code (Claude Code). Claude Code wrote the Notebook system, the inner-voice hint system, and the Notebook screens as scripts for Godot. The Lead Programmer tested every step. The files are marked as SI-generated in their code comments.
  • Data and text (Claude Code). Claude Code wrote draft text for the 48 inner-voice hint lines, the 10 Notebook word meanings, and the Notebook screen wording. The Head Writer edits all of it. The NASA numbers in the game were not written by SI. They come from NASA sources, and each one has its source recorded in the game files.
  • Images (ChatGPT image generation). ChatGPT image generation made the color scheme and the character designs of the Scientist Assistant, Janitor, and Student. Each of these images carries a visible “SI-generated” watermark.
  • Audio (Claude Code). Claude Code generated the background music and sound effects in the game.
  • Not made by SI: the game idea, the character ideas and personalities, and the story.
  • NASA branding: no SI-generated content uses or changes any NASA logo, flag or mission identifier.
